newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Tin - Malaysia miners watch helpless as price dives.
newsitem.headline: Tin - Malaysia miners watch helpless as price dives.

text.p: Malaysian tin miners are watching helplessly as the local price of the metal hits new lows and many are bracing for an eventual shutdown of the country's tin mining sector, industry officials said on Friday.
The spot price on the Kuala Lumpur Tin Market slid to a fresh 27-month low of 13.52 ringgit ($5.41) on Friday, after staying at an average of 15.35 ringgit through the whole of last year.
Traders said there was no indication the price -- which almost certainly followed the daily fluctuations on the London Metal Exchange (LME) -- could rebound to last year's level.

"The way I look at it, the current market is just the work of speculators selling both long and short and has absolutely nothing to do with fundamentals," Muhamad Nor Muhamad, chairman of the Malaysian Chamber of Mines (MCM), told Reuters.
"The miners are bleeding...in fact they are bleeding to death," he added.
He said the current price could hardly be described as remunerative, "and if this goes on further, more tin mines could close".
The MCM, an umbrella body for miners in Malaysia, estimates there are about 40 tin mines left in the country, compared to hundreds that existed before a global tin slump began in 1985.
Production of tin has fallen from a high of 76,800 tonnes in 1972 to 5,174 tonnes last year, MCM said.
It said last year alone, the production value of tin fell eight million ringgit to 80 million.
"The outlook doesn't look good at all," said a spokesman for a key tin smelting company in Malaysia.
He said if the price continued to tumble, local mines might be driven out of the business altogether "and this will make the raw material more expensive".
"Even now, we are importing our supplies from overseas," he added.
Malaysia's booming electronics sector was the largest domestic consumer of smelted tin last year, using nearly 56 percent of Malaysia's tin ore output to solder components to circuit boards.
The canning industry was the second largest user at 16 percent.
Malaysia was the world's top tin producer two decades ago, providing a third of global output until the 1980s.
But the crash of the world tin market in 1985 after a glut in production ended the good times for the local tin industry, which now contributes less than three percent of world output.

Muhamad Nor said Malaysia once toyed with the idea of setting up a buffer stock to support local tin prices. "But seeing the way the prices are going, nobody in the right sense of mind will want to pursue this now."
